match.reason: None of the bank points teaches how language changes over time through technology and cultural contact; they cover identity and slang, subject-specific meanings, spelling strategies, and word parts.

draft.title: How language changes
card: English keeps changing. New words arrive, and old words gain new meanings.
new inventions need new words. Words such as selfie and podcast arrived with new devices and apps. Old words can also gain new meanings: cloud now also means online storage.
when English speakers meet people who speak other languages, words are borrowed. Pyjamas came from Hindi and kangaroo came from an Aboriginal language.
The old meaning of a word often stays alongside the new one. Context, the words around it, shows which meaning is used.
draft.remember: English changes as new things and new contacts bring new words and meanings.

a.q: Which sentence uses the word mouse in a meaning that arrived with computers?
opts: Ravi clicked the mouse to open the file
A mouse nibbled the cheese in the pantry
The mouse ran under the old kitchen cupboard
Ella saw a small mouse in the garden shed
a.why: Computers gave the old word mouse a new meaning, a handheld device used to click. The other three sentences use the older meaning, a small animal.
a.clue: Which sentence is about a computer?

b.q: Sam's grandfather says a bug is an insect. Sam says her laptop has a bug. Which statement best explains the difference?
opts: Technology has given an old word a new meaning
One of them has used the word incorrectly
The word was borrowed from another language
The old meaning of bug has now disappeared
b.why: Computers gave bug a new meaning, a fault in a program, while the old meaning stays in use. The old meaning has not disappeared, because Sam's grandfather still uses it, and neither speaker is wrong.
b.clue: Both meanings are still used today.

a.best: Ravi clicked the mouse to open the file

b.best: Technology has given an old word a new meaning
